name: Urea cycle disorder
aliases: hyperammonaemia from urea cycle enzyme deficiency

reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: A group of inherited defects in enzymes or transporters of the urea cycle that impair conversion of ammonia to urea, causing hyperammonaemia
Severe neonatal presentation is typically a well baby who develops poor feeding, lethargy, vomiting, tachypnoea and encephalopathy in the first days of life
The hallmark biochemical finding is hyperammonaemia usually with a respiratory alkalosis and, in most defects, a normal anion gap (distinguishing from organic acidaemias)
Plasma citrulline and urine orotic acid help localise the enzymatic block within the cycle
Later-onset and partial defects can present in older children or adults with episodic encephalopathy, psychiatric symptoms, or protein aversion, often triggered by catabolic stress

Acute management principles are to stop protein intake, reverse catabolism with high calorie (glucose and lipid) support, and lower ammonia with nitrogen-scavenging agents and, when severe, haemodialysis
Arginine (or citrulline) supplementation is used to replenish urea cycle intermediates in most defects except arginase deficiency
Many urea cycle disorders are included in newborn screening panels, though the most severe neonatal cases may present before results return
reference.pathophysiology: The urea cycle detoxifies waste nitrogen by converting ammonia derived from amino acid metabolism into urea for renal excretion. Deficiency of any of its enzymes (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1, ornithine transcarbamylase, argininosuccinate synthetase, argininosuccinate lyase, arginase) or of the N-acetylglutamate synthase activator or transporters interrupts this flux, causing ammonia to accumulate. Ammonia is neurotoxic, producing astrocyte swelling, cerebral oedema and glutamine accumulation, leading to encephalopathy and, if untreated, irreversible brain injury or death. The pattern of accumulated intermediates (citrulline, argininosuccinate) and urine orotic acid reflects the position of the block.
additionalDifferentials: Organic acidaemias (which cause hyperammonaemia with metabolic acidosis)
additionalInvestigations: Plasma ammonia (urgent) and arterial blood gas showing respiratory alkalosis
Plasma amino acids (citrulline, arginine, argininosuccinate) and urine orotic acid to localise the defect
Plasma glucose, lactate, and acid-base status to distinguish from organic acidaemias
Enzyme assays and molecular genetic testing for the specific defect
Neuroimaging to assess cerebral oedema in severe hyperammonaemia
redFlags: Severe hyperammonaemia with encephalopathy is a medical emergency requiring immediate ammonia-lowering and often dialysis
Rapidly declining level of consciousness, seizures, or signs of raised intracranial pressure from cerebral oedema
Neonate deteriorating after an initially normal period, mistaken for sepsis
Recurrent unexplained encephalopathy or coma triggered by high protein intake, infection, or surgery in older patients
reference.prognosis: Outcome correlates strongly with the peak and duration of hyperammonaemia; prolonged severe neonatal hyperammonaemia carries a high risk of death or permanent neurodevelopmental impairment, whereas early recognition, prompt ammonia control and liver transplantation in selected cases improve survival and reduce disability.
pitfalls: Failing to measure ammonia in an encephalopathic neonate or child and attributing symptoms to sepsis
Allowing sample delay or poor technique to give falsely elevated or unreliable ammonia results
Continuing protein intake or under-treating catabolism during acute decompensation
Not recognising milder late-onset presentations, especially in females with ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency
management: Institute lifelong dietary protein restriction with essential amino acid supplements and high non-protein calorie intake to limit waste-nitrogen production and prevent catabolism
Give nitrogen-scavenging drugs (sodium benzoate and sodium or glycerol phenylbutyrate) to provide alternative pathways for nitrogen excretion
Supplement arginine or citrulline according to the specific enzymatic block (avoiding arginine in arginase deficiency)

Treat acute hyperammonaemic crises by stopping protein, reversing catabolism with intravenous glucose with or without insulin and intravenous lipid, and giving intravenous nitrogen scavengers and arginine
Escalate to haemodialysis or haemofiltration for severe or refractory hyperammonaemia, and consider liver transplantation as definitive therapy in severe or recurrently decompensating disease
Monitor plasma ammonia, plasma amino acids, growth and neurodevelopment, and provide a written emergency sick-day regimen while avoiding sodium valproate and other catabolic triggers

Coordinate care through a metabolic medicine team with specialist dietetic support, and offer genetic counselling and family screening (X-linked for ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, otherwise autosomal recessive)
